literal: While a guest is outside, eating by oneself, even if it is the medicine of immortality, is not a thing to be desired.
translation: Even if it is the nectar of immortality that prevents death, eating it alone while a guest is kept waiting outside is not a worthy thing to do.
modern: விருந்தினர் வெளியே இருக்கும்போது, தான் மட்டும் தனியாக உண்பது, அது சாகா வரம் தரும் அமிழ்தமாகவே இருந்தாலும், விரும்பத்தக்கது அன்று.
explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of hospitality. It argues that even if one possesses 'cāvā maruntu'—the legendary nectar of immortality that prevents death—it is improper to consume it alone while a guest is waiting outside. The key contrast is between 'viruntu' (guest) being outside ('puṟattatā') and 'tāṉ uṇṭal' (eating by oneself). By using the most precious substance imaginable as an example, the poet emphasizes that sharing food with others takes absolute precedence over one's own self-preservation.
